paragraphs: The following assessments concern how materials scientists conduct research and development. They do not predict hiring, qualifications, authorization, or research results.

Materials scientists focus on understanding and improving materials: studying the structure and properties of metals, alloys, polymers, ceramics, and other materials to support new products or improve existing ones; testing strength, strength-to-weight ratio, ductility, magnetic and electrical properties, and resistance to wear, corrosion, heat, and cold; testing samples under tension, compression, and shear to determine causes of failure; identifying ways to strengthen or combine materials or developing materials with new properties; planning laboratory tests to verify process feasibility; developing test methods and conducting experiments and computer modeling to study material structure and responses to forces; writing reports and papers; and recommending reliable materials for different environments.

Entirely fictional task package: Provide fictional data on material structure and performance, including 1 set of application and performance requirements, 1 set of test and modeling data, and 1 failure or performance shortfall to explain. Within 60 minutes, write research hypotheses, a testing and modeling plan, candidate materials or strengthening approaches, verification methods, and limitations. Do not use real company, product, or confidential data.

Sample output and reflection: Check whether you first defined application and performance requirements, explained data and test conditions, distinguished observations from hypotheses, and documented verification and limitations. Then ask yourself whether you can sustain work on experiments and literature, honestly acknowledge insufficient data, and take responsibility for research conclusions and safety.

Materials scientists on this page refers to O*NET 19-2032.00: professionals who study the structure and chemical properties of natural, synthetic, or composite materials, including metals, alloys, rubber, ceramics, semiconductors, polymers, and glass; identify methods of strengthening or combining materials; or develop materials with new properties for various products and applications. Titles include glass scientist, ceramic scientist, metallurgical scientist, and polymer scientist. Work includes studying material structure and properties, testing mechanical and electrical performance, identifying strengthening or combining methods, planning laboratory tests, writing reports and papers, recommending materials, supervising production processes, studying material characteristics through experiments and modeling, and developing test methods. Work is mainly in laboratories, R&D centers, and offices. This page excludes adjacent occupations such as biomedical engineers, chemical engineers, electrical engineers, electronics engineers, and industrial engineers.

entries: Work inputs: Application and performance requirements, material systems and samples, testing and inspection equipment, modeling and computing tools, literature and standards, process and manufacturing cost constraints, safety and compliance requirements, and client and funder needs.

Verifiable outputs: Research hypotheses and testing plans, structure and performance data, failure and mechanism analyses, strengthening or composite approaches, proposals for new materials or applications, papers and reports, test methods, and material selection recommendations for different environments.

Complete workflow: Define application and performance requirements → review literature and develop hypotheses → plan and conduct tests and modeling → analyze structure and performance data → propose material or process solutions → verify and document findings to complete the cycle.

paragraphs: Key judgments: Whether application and performance requirements are clear, test and modeling conditions are reliable, conclusions have sufficient data support, solutions balance performance, cost, and safety, and conclusions stay within research and authorization boundaries.

Environment and pace: Mainly controlled indoor laboratories, with daily email use and frequent meetings and discussions, emphasizing precision and teamwork. Work centers on research, testing, and documentation. Most work around 40 hours a week and may encounter contaminants, hazardous conditions, and equipment.

Research inputs: Occupational identity, tasks, work activities, work context, skills and knowledge, interest code, education, and Job Zone for O*NET 19-2032.00. Wage, employment, and industry data on that page cover this occupation. Research findings are not used to infer qualifications, pay, or employment definitions in mainland China.

Check first: Application and performance requirements, test and modeling conditions, definitions used in data and literature, safety and compliance requirements, cost and capacity constraints, and the strength of evidence and authorization boundaries for conclusions.

Work cycle: Start by defining application and performance requirements, then review literature and develop hypotheses, conduct testing and modeling, analyze data, propose material or process solutions, verify them, and document findings. Do not draw conclusions before confirming all test conditions and data definitions, or apply findings before checking every safety and compliance boundary.

Boundaries with adjacent roles: This page covers only materials scientists. Biomedical engineers work in medical engineering; chemical engineers handle chemical processes; electrical and electronics engineers handle electrical and electronic systems; industrial engineers handle production systems. Judgments and authorizations in these specialties are not interchangeable with those described here.

Biomedical engineers work on medical and biological engineering. Materials scientists study material structure and properties and must collaborate with biomedical engineering when working on medical materials.
Chemical engineers handle chemical processes and equipment. Materials scientists study material structure and performance and develop new materials, with different objectives and methods.

Electrical engineers handle electrical systems and equipment. Materials scientists focus on materials themselves and must collaborate with electrical engineering on conclusions involving materials with electrical properties.
Industrial engineers handle production systems and efficiency. Materials scientists conduct materials research and development and do not take responsibility for production system design.
Boundaries of AI impact on materials scientists

Editorial task hypothesis: Material simulations, spectrum analysis algorithms, and performance prediction models are distinct from generative AI. The latter may help organize fictional literature summaries or report drafts; occupation-specific adoption rates or job outcomes have not been obtained. Generated spectra or data must not be presented as measurements, and model predictions must not be treated directly as proof of mechanisms. Check original references, raw data, and applicable conditions. Do not upload unpublished findings or formulations without approval. AI Impact Score 58% is an editorial estimate. Occupational sources explain actual tasks and objects of work, including materials and samples, testing and modeling, literature and standards, and reports and recommendations. Tool capabilities, institutional adoption, and job outcomes are recorded separately. Wage or employment data are not substitutes for AI evidence.

Editorial comparison: Drafting may be assisted, but no research establishing the sequence of adoption has been obtained. Traditional modeling and specialized prediction do not prove generative AI adoption. Material mechanisms require support from experiments and reproducible analysis.

Human control points: Define research questions and hypotheses, assess test and modeling conditions, honestly acknowledge insufficient data, take responsibility for new-material proposals and safety compliance, and follow research ethics and authorization boundaries.

First conduct an offline exercise using entirely fictional material structure and performance data. Write research hypotheses, a testing and modeling plan, and verification boundaries without relying on unverified automated analysis to replace research judgment.
Editorial hypothesis: Documentation and literature organization may be assisted; adoption rates and job replacement evidence have not been obtained.

Retain original spectra, sample and batch information, and test conditions, and check references and data processing. Label fictional exercises clearly; do not publish them as experimental results or use them as proof of product safety.

Fit signals: Start with observable work behaviors

To assess fit, first consider whether you can turn application needs into research hypotheses and testing plans, patiently conduct tests and rigorously analyze data and spectra, honestly acknowledge insufficient data, sustain literature reading and writing, and collaborate across engineering and production. Tools such as RIASEC can only generate hypotheses and cannot replace real task experience.

Positive signals: Developing testable hypotheses, rigorously analyzing test and modeling data, sustaining literature reading and writing, treating uncertainty honestly, and collaborating with multiple parties.

Reasons for caution: Difficulty sustaining repetitive experiments and literature work, a tendency to draw conclusions without sufficient data, reluctance to write and communicate, or difficulty adapting to laboratory safety requirements and hazardous conditions.

Trial action: Using entirely fictional material structure and performance data, practice developing research hypotheses and a testing and modeling plan, then ask someone else to review it against your records.

The O*NET interest code is IRC (Investigative–Realistic–Conventional): an inclination toward research and analysis, hands-on testing, and organizing information according to procedures. These labels describe activity preferences only and do not determine competence or qualifications.

General personality measures such as the Big Five do not provide job-specific evidence for this occupation and can only support self-reflection. Continue checking through actual materials testing, data analysis, and paper-writing experience.
Type tools such as MBTI and the Enneagram cannot determine competence or qualifications and can only support self-reflection.

Entry pathways and capability stages

O*NET's survey of education for new hires reports 62% bachelor's, 14% doctoral, and 10% master's degrees; these are not mandatory thresholds for every position. The several years of preparation in JobZone4 describe the group. BLS indicates that chemistry and materials science positions typically require a relevant bachelor's degree, while some research positions require master's or doctoral degrees and may require work experience. Do not treat group preparation years as a prerequisite of multiple years of work for every entry-level role.

In the U.S., a relevant materials, chemistry, or physics bachelor's degree plus laboratory practice is typical; some research positions require master's or doctoral degrees. Check equipment training against the employer's actual equipment. This review did not establish an exact, uniform qualification correspondence in China. Ordinary research reports do not universally constitute statutory testing or safety appraisals. For regulated testing or sign-off, separately verify institutional and personnel authorization; a degree does not automatically grant it.

Degrees, professional certifications, employer equipment training, and authority for regulated testing or safety sign-off are separate. Not all research conclusions require a uniform license. When statutory testing or external sign-off is involved, first check applicable regulations and institutional authorization; this page and paper-based work samples cannot grant it.

Entry stage: Under supervision, practice material preparation and testing, data and spectrum analysis, literature reading and documentation, basic modeling, and writing. Learn safety and research ethics requirements and retain process records.

Evidence to show: Use a reviewable research deliverable describing the question and hypotheses, test and modeling methods, data conclusions, and limitations to demonstrate structured research and honest documentation.

Next step: Check the target employer's materials focus and equipment conditions, publication and intellectual property requirements, and safety and compliance constraints. Verify testing, analysis, and writing skills in supervised real projects.

Progression to greater responsibility: With experience, you may lead independent research projects, mentor others, collaborate in teams, develop a specialty, or move into R&D management, processes, or testing.

Older figures of 8,700 employed in 2024 and 600 average annual openings in 2024–2034 are retained. Latest figures are 8,600 employed in 2025, 8% growth in 2025–2035, and 600 average annual openings—not a period total, a net increase of 700, or current job postings.

The main industries on that page for 2024 are Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services and Manufacturing. Employment and openings are statistical projections and must be interpreted separately from individual opportunities.

Transferable capabilities: Materials and test methods, data and spectrum analysis, modeling and computing, literature searches and writing, failure and mechanism assessment, interdisciplinary communication, and project management.

First target, biomedical engineer: Build knowledge of engineering design and biological systems, medical device and implant material applications, safety and effectiveness verification, and collaboration with clinical and manufacturing teams. BLS indicates a relevant engineering bachelor's degree is typical, with graduate degrees for some positions. Materials structure research does not directly demonstrate competence in medical device development or authorization for clinical diagnosis and treatment.

Source use notes: O*NET 19-2032.00 Materials Scientists (Summary): Provides occupational identity, official description, interest code, Job Zone, skills, and knowledge for 19-2032.00.; Wage and employment data on that page cover this occupation.; O*NET 19-2032.00 Tasks: Provides a task list including studying material structure and properties, testing mechanical and electrical performance, identifying strengthening or combining methods, planning laboratory tests, writing reports and papers, recommending materials, supervising production processes, and developing test methods.; The task sample does not mean every position performs every task.; O*NET 19-2032.00 Work Context: Describes primarily controlled indoor settings, daily communication by email and meetings, an emphasis on precision and teamwork, and possible exposure to contaminants, hazardous conditions, and equipment.; U.S. work context does not replace Chinese law or employer procedures.; O*NET 19-2032.00 National Wages (BLS OEWS display): Median wage from 2025 BLS OEWS; the page covers this occupation.; Percentile wages are not displayed on this page.; O*NET 19-2032.00 National Employment Trends: Employment size in 2024, growth in 2024–2034 (faster than average at 5%–6%), and projected job openings.; Projections are not hiring guarantees.; Industries: 19-2032.00: The main industries on that page for 2024 are Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services and Manufacturing.; Industry distribution signals employer settings, not projected growth or demand.; O*NET 19-2032.00 Education and Career Preparation: Job Zone 4: Most positions require a four-year bachelor's degree (about 62%), while some require a doctorate (about 14%) or master's degree (about 10%).; The education distribution does not constitute mandatory requirements for every employer.; Licenses & Certifications: 19-2032.00: State licensing and national certification search tools provided by O*NET.; Certification and training do not equal authorization to practice or employer hiring requirements.; Generative AI and Jobs (ILO Working Paper 140, 2025): Assesses occupational exposure to generative AI at the task level.; The exposure index does not equal adoption rates, job outcomes, or hiring probabilities.; Average Annual Wages of Persons Employed in Urban Units in 2025: Provides average annual wages by broad industry category for urban non-private and private units, including scientific research and technical services.; An industry average is not an occupational median and excludes individual businesses and freelancers.; FermatMind Materials Scientists Task Impact Scale: Organizes tasks that can be assisted and human control points for task-level discussions of AI and fit.; This editorial scale is not evidence of adoption rates, layoffs, regulations, or licensing.;

subject.name: Materials Scientists
subject.summary: Materials scientists on this page refers to O*NET 19-2032.00: professionals who study the structure and chemical properties of natural, synthetic, or composite materials, including metals, alloys, rubber, ceramics, semiconductors, polymers, and glass; identify methods of strengthening or combining materials; or develop materials with new properties. Titles include glass, ceramic, metallurgical, and polymer scientist.
